title: Adaptive NCCL ring reconfiguration: exploratory log
body:
Purpose and quick TL;DR:

This doc captures an exploratory series of microbenchmarks and prototype patches that try to answer: can we improve multi-tenant, multi-GPU throughput and tail latency by adaptively reconfiguring NCCL channel/ring layouts at runtime based on observed link contention and per-request bandwidth needs?

TL;DR: On our 8x A100 (NVLink mesh) testbed with synthetic mixed-size traffic, a simple reactive reconfiguration (switch from single ring to split dual rings when cross-node link utilization > 65%) reduced p99 step latency by ~18% for medium-long sequences and increased sustained throughput by ~12% in noisy co-scheduled scenarios. Best gains were when using short measurement windows (50ms) and smoothing over 3 windows. There are trade-offs: reconfigs add microbursts and can temporarily increase jitter; the mechanism needs guardrails (rate-limiting, minimum dwell time).

Motivation / background:
- Existing NCCL channel/ring choices are static or selected at init time. With multi-tenant workloads and asynchronous arrival patterns, the optimal topology can vary by workload mix and by transient link contention (hot NVLink lanes, PCIe transfers).
- Prior logs focused on hierarchical vs flat topologies; we want to experiment with dynamic reconfiguration heuristics that can be applied without full model restart and ideally with minimal correctness/consistency complexity.

Hypothesis:
- If we can detect when a subset of links is saturated or suffering high packet latency, we can reassign NCCL channels (split/merge rings or re-order ranks) to steer heavy inter-GPU paths to less-contended links and reduce queuing stalls.
- For workloads with imbalanced tensor sizes (e.g., KV cache updates + long attention matrices), adaptive channel assignment yields benefits vs static configuration.

Testbed and harness:
- Hardware: 8x NVIDIA A100 (40GB), DGX-style topology: NVLink clos network; two host sockets; PCIe x16 between host and some GPUs.
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 12.2, NCCL 2.18 (patched), driver 535.54.03
- Baseline runtime: serving-runtime commit 0f9bd2 (hybrid-shard branch).
- Measurement nodes: Prometheus + eBPF counters for per-link bytes/s (host-exporter), nvlink counters polled via nvidia-smi dmon + custom NVML wrapper.
- Workloads: mix of short-chat (seq_len 64, batch=8), medium-gen (seq_len 512, batch=1), long-gen (seq_len 2048, batch=1). Arrival: Poisson mix; 30% short, 50% medium, 20% long.
- Co-scheduling noise: synthetic memcpy storms from a background process copying large blobs between host and GPU memory on randomly selected GPUs to create link contention.

Prototype approach:
1) Measurement: 20ms sampling of per-link throughput (bytes/s) and packet latency proxy (nvlink tx stall counters).
2) Heuristic: if any link > 65% of measured peak (sustained for 2 consecutive windows) OR tx_stall > threshold, mark topology as "contended".
3) Reconfig options (applied via patched NCCL runtime APIs we exposed):
   - merge: single-ring (default)
   - split-2: split into two disjoint rings to reduce per-ring hop counts and allow different rings to favor different physical channels
   - rotate-ranks: reorder ranks to change which physical NVLink hops are used for heavy pairs
4) Safety: require min-dwell 250ms between reconfigs; apply reconfig only when average queued requests > 2 to avoid flapping.

Experiments run:
A) Baseline static single-ring under noise (no reconfig). 6x runs, 60s each.
B) Reactive reconfig (split-2 when contended) with measurement window 20ms. 6x runs.
C) Same as B but window 50ms + smoothing 3 windows. 6x runs.
D) Aggressive reconfig (min-dwell 50ms) to observe instability. 4x runs.

Metrics we collected (per-run aggregates):
- step latency p50/p90/p99 (ms) for medium and long sequences
- throughput (tokens/s)
- reconfig count and average reconfig duration (ms)
- temporary spike magnitude (max latency delta within 200ms after reconfig)

Raw results summary (representative):
- Baseline (A): medium p99 = 127ms, long p99 = 742ms, tokens/s = 18.2k
- Reactive 20ms (B): medium p99 = 106ms (-16%), long p99 = 643ms (-13%), tokens/s = 19.7k (+8%)
- Reactive 50ms smooth3 (C): medium p99 = 104ms (-18%), long p99 = 604ms (-19%), tokens/s = 20.4k (+12%)
- Aggressive (D): unstable, frequent reconfigs (avg 18/min), short-lived improvements but average p99 slightly worse than A due to reconfig-induced spikes.

Observations / interpretation:
- The reactive split-2 option is effective when a small subset of links carry disproportionate load; splitting reduces per-hop contention and KV cache update concurrency interference.
- Longer smoothing window (50ms x3) reduced false positives and avoided useless reconfig churn, which produced the best stable gains.
- Aggressive policies that try to chase every transient spike make things worse; reconfig cost (lock+sync) matters for latency-sensitive workloads.
- Reconfigs themselves create microbursts: we saw 1-3% of requests have a >2x latency spike within 100ms post-reconfig. This is visible in p999 and in tail jitter metrics.
- Rank rotation helped in a few runs where topology/physical wiring caused repeated saturation on a particular NVLink pair; it requires good mapping between logical ranks and physical paths (we lacked automated discovery, used static mapping heuristics).

Implementation notes / patches:
- Implemented a small NCCL shim that exposes reconfig commands via an RPC from serving runtime -> NCCL coordinator process. This is hacky but sufficient for experiments. Code in PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/987.
- Needed additional NVML counters to detect tx_stall; on older drivers these counters aren't visible so fallback to link occupancy heuristics.
- Reconfig path required short quiesce: we pause driver's collective submission for the GPUs involved, rearrange ring/channel assignment, and resume. Took ~8-14ms in our implementation (majority serialization overhead).

Risks and open questions:
- Consistency: we must ensure KV-cache and per-request causal dependencies aren't violated by rank reorder. In our tests we handled by pausing new requests for GPUs undergoing reconfig; this introduces latency but is simpler. For production we need a lockless approach or per-request routing to bypass reconfig window.
- Cross-cloud / different topologies: results are NVLink-dominant; PCIe-heavy topologies may need different heuristics. Additional mapping required per-hardware family.
- Security/tenant isolation: reconfig policies could be gamed by a noisy tenant. Consider rate-limits on tenant-triggered reconfig or per-tenant meters.

Actionable next steps:
- (WIP) Implement a lightweight non-blocking rank-rotation that uses staggered channel flips to minimize pause window (prototype #2).
- Add per-tenant scorecard and tie reconfig approvals to SLO tiers (prevent noisy low-tier tenants from forcing reconfigs).
- Run longer 24h soak with more varied arrival patterns and real inference traces (customer-anon).
- Improve physical mapping discovery: add a small calibration pass on startup to identify which logical pairs map to which NVLink lanes and their baseline capacity.
- Instrumentation: add histogram of latency spikes centered on reconfig events and publish dashboard in Console (model-level view).

Notes to self / rough TODOs:
- Record detailed Wireshark-like NCcl traces for the two runs that showed best p99 improvement; look for packet retrans patterns.
- File a ticket to infra for creating a PCIe-heavy testbed to validate behavior under different interconnect balance. (JIRA-RT-4138)
- Share results with SRE and Perf guild next Thurs (prep slides + one-page).

Appendix: selected command snippets used to drive experiments:
- start background noise:
  python tools/gpu_memcpy_storm.py --gpus 1,3,5 --size 8G --interval 0.12
- poll nvlink counters (toy):
  watch -n 0.02 ./tools/nvlink_probe.sh | grep TX_BYTES
- reconfig rpc (toy):
  curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:9080/reconfig -d '{"mode":"split-2"}'

End of log for now. Comments welcome, especially on safer reconfig coordination designs or alternate heuristics (capacity-proportional split, channel-weighted round robin).

Signed-off: Aisha P.
